Jehoshaphat refused to cooperate, so Ahaziah built the ships on his own
The ships were wrecked because Jehoshaphat had allied himself with a wicked king
explanation: According to 2 Chronicles 20:35-37, Jehoshaphat allied himself with Ahaziah, who did wickedly, to build ships to go to Tarshish; the prophet Eliezer rebuked him, saying that because he had allied himself with Ahaziah, the LORD had destroyed his works, and the ships were wrecked and were not able to go to Tarshish. (1) is correct in both outcome and reason. (2) 'Sailing to Ophir to bring back gold' refers to the successful voyage during Solomon's time, wrong scope (wrong_scope, almost-right). (3) 'The Philistines burning the ships' is a fabricated cause — the text says the ships were wrecked by divine judgment (wrong_detail, almost-right). (4) 'Refusing to cooperate' contradicts the text since he had already allied himself before being rebuked (wrong_detail).

content: When Jehoram became king of Judah and had established himself over his kingdom, what did he do to his own brothers?
options: He killed all his brothers with the sword
He exiled them to Edom as forced laborers
He gave them control over the fortified cities
He forced them to worship the Baals
explanation: According to 2 Chronicles 21:4, when Jehoram had established himself over his father's kingdom, he 'put all his brothers to the sword, and also some of the princes of Israel', so the correct answer is that he killed all his brothers with the sword. (1) 'Exiling them to Edom as forced laborers' is a wrong detail — Edom only appears in 21:8 when it rebelled against Judah (wrong_detail). (2) 'Giving them control over the fortified cities' reverses the text — it was his father Jehoshaphat who distributed the cities to his sons (21:3) (near_passage). (3) 'Forcing them to worship the Baals' is confused with Jehoram building high places and leading Judah into spiritual prostitution (21:11), which was not directed at his brothers (wrong_scope).

content: During Jehoram's reign over Judah, the king received a warning letter rebuking him for his sins. Which prophet sent that letter?
options: The prophet Elijah
The prophet Elisha
The prophet Isaiah
The prophet Jehu
explanation: According to 2 Chronicles 21:12, 'a letter came to him from Elijah the prophet', warning of the disaster that would come upon the king and his people, so the correct answer is Elijah. (1) 'Elisha' was Elijah's successor; they are easily confused because they were contemporaries and their names are similar (common_misconception). (2) 'Isaiah' was a prophet active during the reigns of later kings such as Hezekiah, placing him in the wrong era (wrong_scope). (3) 'Jehu son of Hanani' was the one who rebuked Jehoshaphat, Jehoram's father (19:2) — close to this passage but the wrong person (near_passage).

content: Ahaziah, king of Judah, was the maternal grandson of a famously wicked king of Israel. What was Ahaziah's mother's name?
options: Athaliah
Jezebel
Maacah
Jehoshabeath
explanation: According to 2 Chronicles 22:2, Ahaziah's mother was 'Athaliah, the daughter of Omri', and she counseled him to do wickedly, so the correct answer is Athaliah. (1) 'Jezebel' was his grandmother (wife of Ahab and mother of Athaliah); she is easily confused with Athaliah because they belong to the same wicked lineage (common_misconception). (2) 'Maacah' was the queen mother during the reign of King Asa in an earlier period, placing her in the wrong dynasty (wrong_scope). (3) 'Jehoshabeath' was the one who later hid the infant Joash (22:11) — close to this passage but a different role entirely (near_passage).

content: Joash began his reign over Judah at a very young age. How old was he when he became king?
options: Seven years old
Eight years old
Twelve years old
Twenty-five years old
explanation: According to 2 Chronicles 24:1, 'Joash was seven years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem', so the correct answer is seven years old. (1) 'Eight years old' was the age at which Josiah became king (34:1) — the same type of detail but the wrong number (wrong_detail). (2) 'Twelve years old' was the age of Manasseh when he began to reign (33:1) — a different king confused with Joash (wrong_scope). (3) 'Twenty-five years old' was the age of Jotham when he became king — yet another king of Judah's accession age (wrong_detail).

content: Elijah's prophecy warned that Jehoram would be struck with a severe illness. How does the text describe the final affliction that came upon Jehoram's body?
options: His bowels were in agony from an incurable disease and eventually came out, and he died
He was struck with leprosy on his forehead and remained so until his death
He became severely lame from a foot disease and then died
He suffered a stroke, became mute, and died in the palace
explanation: According to 2 Chronicles 21:18–19, the LORD 'struck him in his bowels with an incurable disease', and at the end 'in the course of time, at the end of two years, his bowels came out because of the disease, and he died in great agony'. The correct answer specifically describes the bowels coming out. (1) 'Leprosy on his forehead' is what happened to King Uzziah when he unlawfully burned incense (26:19–20) — an almost-right distractor because it is also a divine judgment through disease, but it involves the wrong illness and the wrong king (near_passage). (2) 'Severe foot disease' was the illness that afflicted King Asa (16:12) — a different king confused with Jehoram (wrong_scope). (3) 'A stroke rendering him mute' is a fabricated detail with no basis in the text about Jehoram (wrong_detail).

content: Ahaziah king of Judah was killed during Jehu's purge. Why does the text say he was still given a proper burial even though he died at the hands of an enemy?
options: Because he was a grandson of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD with all his heart
Because he repented and returned to the LORD before he died
Because he was the legitimate anointed king of the house of David
Because his mother Athaliah pleaded with Jehu to spare his body
explanation: According to 2 Chronicles 22:9, he was buried because it was said that 'he was the son of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD with all his heart,' so the correct answer gives the reason as descent from the God-fearing Jehoshaphat (the word 'son' here refers to a descendant). (1) 'He repented and returned before he died' sounds pious, but the text says he did evil following the house of Ahab (22:4) and shows no repentance (true_but_off). (2) 'The legitimate anointed king of the house of David' is a generally plausible reason but is not the reason the text gives (true_but_off). (3) 'His mother Athaliah pleaded with Jehu' is a fabricated detail — Athaliah was in Jerusalem and never met Jehu (wrong_detail).

content: The priest Jehoiada organized a coup to put Joash on the throne. According to the text, who were the main forces he summoned and made a covenant with to carry out the plan?
options: The commanders of hundreds, the Levites, and the heads of families
The entire standing army of the kingdom of Judah
Prophets and diviners summoned from throughout the land
The mercenary troops of the Cherethites and Pelethites
explanation: According to 2 Chronicles 23:1-2, Jehoiada 'made a covenant with the commanders of hundreds' and sent them to gather 'the Levites... and the heads of families of Israel' to Jerusalem, so the correct answer names the commanders of hundreds, the Levites, and the heads of families. (1) 'The entire standing army' is almost right, but the text focuses on the commanders of hundreds rather than a national army corps (wrong_detail). (2) 'Prophets and diviners' play no part in Jehoiada's plan (wrong_detail). (3) 'The mercenary Cherethites and Pelethites' were David's royal guard — wrong era entirely (wrong_scope).

content: After the priest Jehoiada died, King Joash turned against him and ordered the stoning of a prophet right in the court of the temple. What was this victim's relationship to Jehoiada?
options: He was Zechariah, the son of Jehoiada
He was Zechariah, the grandson of Jehoiada
He was Azariah, a fellow priest of Jehoiada
He was Obed, a Levite disciple of Jehoiada
explanation: According to 2 Chronicles 24:20-22, 'Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest' rebuked the people, and Joash 'did not remember the kindness that Jehoiada, Zechariah's father, had shown him' but killed the son of his benefactor. The correct answer is son. (1) 'Grandson of Jehoiada' is off by exactly one degree of relationship — almost right (wrong_detail). (2) 'Azariah the fellow priest' is a different priestly figure in Chronicles (26:17) — wrong person (wrong_scope). (3) 'Obed the Levite disciple' is a completely fabricated detail (wrong_detail).

content: The temple restoration under Joash was initially stalled before finally succeeding. Compared to the original collection method, what change ultimately brought the project to completion?
options: A chest was placed outside the temple gate for the people to deposit silver themselves, instead of sending Levites to collect it
The king ordered the temple tax to be doubled per capita throughout the land of Judah
Joash drew silver from his own royal treasury to make up what the people had not contributed
The priests were put in direct charge of the silver and took responsibility for hiring the workers themselves
explanation: According to 2 Chronicles 24:5-11, the Levites were first sent to collect silver but 'did not act quickly'; the king then commanded that 'a chest be made and set outside the gate of the house of the LORD' so the people could deposit silver 'according to the requirement of Moses,' and enough was gathered to finish the work (24:8-13). The correct answer identifies the chest placed at the gate as the replacement for the Levites going out to collect. (1) 'Doubling the tax' is a fabricated detail — the text speaks only of the Mosaic requirement with no increase (wrong_detail). (2) 'Joash drawing from the royal treasury' sounds plausible, but the text shows the silver came from the people through the chest, not from the king's stores (true_but_off). (3) 'Priests keeping the silver and hiring workers directly' reverses the text — the slowness of the Levites and priests was the original problem, and the silver was handed over to overseers of the work (24:12); almost right but the mechanism is wrong (near_passage).

content: The chronicler emphasizes that Jehoram did evil like the house of Israel rather than following the example of his father. What reason does the text give to explain why he followed the ways of the house of Ahab?
options: Because he married a daughter of Ahab as his wife
Because he formed a military alliance with the king of Israel against Syria
Because his mother came from the northern royal family
Because prophets of Baal seduced him from his youth
explanation: According to 2 Chronicles 21:6, Jehoram 'walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as the house of Ahab had done, for the daughter of Ahab was his wife,' so the reason the text gives is his marriage to Ahab's daughter. (1) 'A military alliance against Syria' was what his father Jehoshaphat did with Ahab (18:3) — almost right because it also involves the house of Ahab, but it is not the reason given for Jehoram (near_passage). (2) 'His mother came from the northern royal family' confuses this case with Ahaziah, whose mother was Athaliah (22:2-3) — almost right but wrong person and wrong relationship (wrong_scope). (3) 'Baal prophets seducing him from his youth' is a fabricated detail not found in the text (wrong_detail).

content: According to 2 Chronicles 25:1, how old was Amaziah when he became king of Judah?
options: Twenty-five years old
Sixteen years old
Twenty years old
Thirty years old
explanation: 2 Chronicles 25:1 states: 'Amaziah was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem.' 'Sixteen years old' is the age at which Uzziah became king in the following chapter (26:3) (near_passage). 'Twenty years old' and 'Thirty years old' are numbers that do not match the text (wrong_detail).

content: According to 2 Chronicles 25:11-12, which nation did Amaziah defeat at the Valley of Salt?
options: The Edomites (the people of Seir)
The Philistines
The Ammonites
The Arameans (Syrians)
explanation: 2 Chronicles 25:11 records that Amaziah 'went to the Valley of Salt and struck down 10,000 men of Seir,' that is, the Edomites. The Philistines were the enemy that Uzziah defeated (26:6) (near_passage). The Ammonites were the people Jotham defeated in chapter 27 (wrong_scope). The Arameans were not the target of this battle (wrong_detail).

content: According to 2 Chronicles 26:3, how many years did Uzziah reign in Jerusalem?
options: Fifty-two years
Twenty-nine years
Sixteen years
Forty years
explanation: 2 Chronicles 26:3 states: 'Uzziah was sixteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem.' 'Twenty-nine years' is the length of Amaziah's reign (25:1) (near_passage). 'Sixteen years' is the number of years Jotham reigned (27:1) and also the age at which Uzziah became king, which can easily cause confusion (common_misconception). 'Forty years' does not match the text (wrong_detail).

content: According to 2 Chronicles 27:1, what was the name of King Jotham's mother?
options: Jerushah, the daughter of Zadok
Jecoliah of Jerusalem
Jehoaddan of Jerusalem
Abijah, the daughter of Zechariah
explanation: 2 Chronicles 27:1 records that Jotham's mother 'was Jerushah the daughter of Zadok.' Jecoliah was the mother of Uzziah (26:3) (near_passage). Jehoaddan was the mother of Amaziah (25:1) (near_passage). 'Abijah the daughter of Zechariah' is a composite name not found in these chapters (wrong_detail).

content: According to 2 Chronicles 25:7-10, why did Amaziah send the hired Israelite troops home even though he had already paid one hundred talents of silver?
options: Because a man of God warned that the LORD was not with Israel, so the king would be defeated in battle
Because the hired soldiers mutinied and demanded higher pay, so the king angrily dismissed them
Because the king feared the added cost of supplying provisions for the army on a long march
Because a prophet argued that Judah's army was already far larger than the enemy's
explanation: 2 Chronicles 25:7-8 records that the man of God said: 'O king, do not let the army of Israel go with you, for the LORD is not with Israel... God will cast you down before the enemy.' The reason was spiritual, not that the soldiers mutinied and demanded more pay (wrong_detail). It was not out of fear of the cost of provisions (wrong_detail). The dismissed soldiers went away in fierce anger and raided the cities of Judah (25:13); the prophet never argued that Judah's army was larger than the enemy's (common_misconception).

content: According to 2 Chronicles 25:14-16, what provoked God's anger against Amaziah after his victory over Edom?
options: The king brought the gods of the people of Seir and set them up as his own gods, bowing down to them and burning offerings to them
The king offered burnt offerings to the LORD without going through the priests
The king kept the plunder of war instead of destroying it according to the ban
The king arrogantly burned incense on the altar in the temple
explanation: 2 Chronicles 25:14 records that after defeating Edom, Amaziah 'brought the gods of the men of Seir and set them up as his gods and worshiped them, making offerings to them.' The king did not properly offer sacrifices to the LORD at all (wrong_detail). The text makes no mention of retaining forbidden plunder (wrong_detail). 'Arrogantly burning incense in the temple' was the sin of Uzziah in the following chapter (26:16), not Amaziah (near_passage).

content: According to 2 Chronicles 26:5, what was the means by which Uzziah sought God and prospered during the early years of his reign?
options: Through Zechariah, who instructed the king in the fear of God
Through the prophet Isaiah, who counseled the king in his early years
Through the priest Azariah, who restrained the king from evil
Through the king's mother Jecoliah, who guided the king in worship
explanation: 2 Chronicles 26:5 records: 'In the days of Zechariah, who instructed him in the fear of God, he sought God, and as long as he sought the LORD, God made him prosper.' Isaiah did minister during this period (Isaiah 6:1), but the text names Zechariah, not Isaiah (true_but_off). The priest Azariah appears when confronting Uzziah over the burning of incense (26:17), not as the one who taught the king to fear God (near_passage). Jecoliah is mentioned only as the king's mother (26:3) and is given no teaching role (wrong_detail).

content: According to 2 Chronicles 27:5, what tribute did Jotham receive from the Ammonites after defeating them?
options: One hundred talents of silver, ten thousand cors of wheat, and ten thousand cors of barley
One hundred talents of silver and one hundred talents of gold paid regularly each year
Seven hundred rams and seven hundred male goats to be offered as sacrifices
One thousand talents of silver along with many flocks of sheep and large herds of camels
explanation: 2 Chronicles 27:5 records that the Ammonites paid Jotham 'one hundred talents of silver, ten thousand cors of wheat, and ten thousand cors of barley' in both the second and third years. 'One hundred talents of gold each year' substitutes gold for silver and omits the grain entirely (wrong_detail). 'Rams and male goats' do not appear in this tribute at all (wrong_detail). 'One thousand talents of silver with flocks and camels' inflates the amount and adds details not present in the text (wrong_detail).

content: According to 2 Chronicles 25:3-4, Amaziah executed the men who had murdered his father but did not put their children to death. What reason does the text give for the king's action?
options: Because the law in the Book of Moses commanded that each person must die for his own sin
Because the king wanted to keep their children as hostages to deter other rebels
Because their children were too young to be brought to trial
Because a prophet advised the king to show mercy in order to win the people's loyalty
explanation: 2 Chronicles 25:4 states the reason explicitly: the king acted according to what was written in the Law, in the Book of Moses, which says, 'Fathers shall not be put to death because of their children, nor children be put to death because of their fathers, but each one shall die for his own sin' (cf. Deuteronomy 24:16). This question requires distinguishing the theological motive from other plausible-sounding reasons. 'Keeping hostages to deter rebels' is a political motive the text never mentions (wrong_detail). 'Too young to stand trial' infers ages from nothing in the context (common_misconception). 'A prophet advised showing mercy to win loyalty' attributes prophetic speech that does not occur here (wrong_detail).

content: Comparing Jotham with his father Uzziah in 2 Chronicles 27:2-6, what specific contrast does the text draw to explain why Jotham grew increasingly strong?
options: Jotham did what was right but did not enter the temple of the LORD as his father had done
Jotham demolished all the high places where his father had permitted the people to offer sacrifices
Jotham himself entered the temple to burn incense before the LORD in place of the priests
Jotham formed an alliance with the king of Israel and thereby gained great military strength
explanation: 2 Chronicles 27:2 records that Jotham 'did what was right in the eyes of the LORD according to all that his father Uzziah had done, but he did not enter the temple of the LORD,' and verse 6 concludes, 'Jotham grew mighty, because he ordered his ways before the LORD his God.' Refraining from entering the temple is precisely the contrast with Uzziah's sin of arrogance (26:16). The text also notes that 'the people still followed corrupt practices' at the high places, so saying Jotham tore them down is wrong (wrong_detail). 'Burning incense in place of the priests' was Uzziah's sin — the direct opposite of what Jotham did (common_misconception). 'Forming an alliance with the king of Israel' is never mentioned and was not the source of Jotham's strength (wrong_scope).

content: Which king of Judah in these chapters is described as doing evil, casting images of the Baals, and burning his sons in fire?
options: Ahaz
Hezekiah
Jotham
Manasseh
explanation: 2 Chronicles 28:1-3 states that Ahaz 'did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD... made metal images for the Baals, made offerings... and burned his sons as an offering.' Hezekiah was Ahaz's son but did what was good (wrong_detail). Jotham was Ahaz's father and did what was right in the eyes of the LORD (near_passage). Manasseh also burned his sons in fire but belonged to a later generation, outside the scope of these chapters (wrong_scope).

content: Because of Ahaz's unfaithfulness, God delivered him into the hands of which kings for punishment?
options: The king of Syria and the king of Israel
The king of Egypt and the king of Moab
The king of Babylon and the king of Assyria
The king of Philistia and the king of Edom
explanation: 2 Chronicles 28:5 records that the LORD 'gave him into the hand of the king of Syria... He was also given into the hand of the king of Israel.' The kings of Babylon and Assyria are connected to other reigns and fall outside this scope (wrong_scope). The Philistines and Edomites did invade Ahaz afterward (28:17-18) but are not the two kings God specifically delivered him into at this verse (near_passage). Egypt and Moab played no part in this conflict (wrong_detail).

content: After the Israelite army captured many captives from Judah, what caused them to change their minds and decide to release the captives?
options: The warning of the prophet Oded that they too were guilty before the LORD
A direct command from Pekah, king of Israel
The Judean army rose up in counterattack and reclaimed the captives
King Ahaz paid a large ransom to redeem his people
explanation: 2 Chronicles 28:9-11 records that the prophet Oded warned the Israelite army: 'you have sinned against the LORD your God,' and urged them to release the captives; then the chiefs of Ephraim responded and took action (28:12-15). King Pekah's direct command is not given as the reason (wrong_detail). The Judean army did not rise up and fight back to reclaim the captives (wrong_scope). Ahaz paid no ransom — the release was an act of repentance by the captors, not a negotiated transaction (common_misconception).

content: In his time of distress, what did Ahaz do in seeking help, demonstrating that he became even more unfaithful?
options: Offered sacrifices to the gods of Damascus that had defeated him
Humbled himself and pleaded with the LORD in the temple
Sought help from the gods of the neighboring Philistines
Consulted mediums and spiritists in the land
explanation: 2 Chronicles 28:22-23 records that 'in the time of his distress he became yet more faithless to the LORD — this same King Ahaz. For he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus that had defeated him,' reasoning that those gods had helped the king of Syria. Humbling himself to pray to the LORD is the direct opposite of what the text describes (common_misconception). The gods of Philistia are not mentioned here even though the Philistines did invade (near_passage). Consulting mediums and spiritists was the sin of another king, not Ahaz in this passage (wrong_scope).

content: What did Ahaz do with the vessels of the house of God and with the doors of the temple?
options: Gathered and smashed them, then shut the doors of the temple
Repaired and restored everything
Gave them to the king of Assyria as tribute
Entrusted them to the priests for safekeeping
explanation: 2 Chronicles 28:24 records that Ahaz 'gathered together the vessels of the house of God and cut in pieces the vessels of the house of God, and he shut the doors of the house of the LORD.' Repairing and restoring was what Hezekiah did afterward — the exact opposite (wrong_detail). Sending tribute to Assyria is a separate matter (28:21 mentions Ahaz took from the temple to give the king of Assyria, but it did not help him), and is not the action described in this verse (near_passage). Entrusting the priests for safekeeping contradicts the act of shutting the temple doors (wrong_scope).

content: What was the very first thing Hezekiah did in the first year, first month of his reign, revealing the priority of his reform?
options: Reopened and repaired the doors of the temple
Destroyed the altars on the high places
Organized the Passover for all the people
Renewed the covenant with the LORD before the people
explanation: 2 Chronicles 29:3 states that 'in the first year of his reign, in the first month, he opened the doors of the house of the LORD and repaired them,' reversing Ahaz's closure of the temple. Destroying the high places came later (2 Chronicles 31), outside the sequence of this verse (wrong_scope). The Passover took place in chapter 30, after the temple had been cleansed (near_passage). Renewing the covenant is mentioned generally in the reform but was not the 'first' action according to this verse (wrong_detail).

content: Which group did Hezekiah summon and command to consecrate themselves in order to cleanse the temple?
options: The Levites and the priests
The officials and the military commanders
The prophets and the gatekeepers
The elders and the tribal leaders
explanation: 2 Chronicles 29:4–5 records that Hezekiah 'gathered the priests and the Levites... and said to them: Hear me, Levites! Now consecrate yourselves, and consecrate the house of the LORD.' Officials and military commanders were not the group entrusted with the cleansing (wrong_detail). Prophets and gatekeepers are not mentioned here (wrong_scope). The tribal elders were involved in planning the Passover in chapter 30, not in this verse (near_passage).

content: Why did Hezekiah and the assembly decide to postpone the Passover to the second month instead of observing it in the first month as the law required?
options: Because not enough priests had consecrated themselves and the people had not yet assembled in time
Because a war had broken out that threatened the northern border of the land
Because the calendar that year had been miscalculated by a full month
Because the king wanted to wait for the northern tribes to send their tribute to the temple first
explanation: 2 Chronicles 30:2–3 states they kept the feast in the second month because 'the priests had not consecrated themselves in sufficient number, and the people had not assembled in Jerusalem.' Border warfare is not given as a reason in the text (wrong_detail). A calendar miscalculation is an inference with no basis in the passage (common_misconception). Waiting for tribute from the northern tribes was not the reason — the king only sent letters inviting them to come for the feast (wrong_scope).

content: Many people from Ephraim and Manasseh ate the Passover without having properly consecrated themselves according to the law. How did Hezekiah respond, and what was the outcome?
options: He prayed for the LORD to pardon all who set their heart to seek God, and the LORD heard him and healed the people
He barred them from the feast until they had completed the proper purification rites
He commanded the Levites to slaughter additional lambs as substitutes for each unclean person
He postponed the entire feast by another month so that everyone could consecrate themselves in time
explanation: 2 Chronicles 30:18–20 records that Hezekiah prayed: 'May the LORD... pardon everyone who sets his heart to seek God,' and 'the LORD heard Hezekiah and healed the people.' Barring them from the feast is almost-right since the Levitical law requires ritual cleanness, but it contradicts the king's actual response of interceding for forgiveness (true_but_off). The Levites slaughtering lambs on behalf of the unclean correctly describes the act of killing the Passover sacrifice in 30:17, but it is not the solution applied to the problem of eating while unclean in this verse (near_passage). Postponing the feast another month is almost-right since the feast had already been moved to the second month, but no second postponement took place (common_misconception).

content: What made the celebration in Jerusalem under Hezekiah so extraordinary that it was compared to the reign of a previous king?
options: The assembly joyfully kept seven additional days, a joy unprecedented in Jerusalem since the days of Solomon
It was the first Passover observed in full accordance with the law since the time of Moses
For the first time all the tribes of Israel were united under one king since the days of David
The king personally offered a thousand oxen as burnt offerings, just as Solomon had done
explanation: 2 Chronicles 30:23–26 records that the whole assembly decided 'to keep the feast seven more days,' and 'since the time of Solomon... there had been nothing like this in Jerusalem.' The comparison to the time of Moses is almost-right, but a later passage (2 Chronicles 35:18 in Josiah's day) is the one that refers back to Samuel and the kings — not this one (true_but_off). The reunion of all tribes since David is an inference not found in the text, even though northerners attended the feast (common_misconception). The offering of a thousand oxen is a detail from Solomon's reign (1 Kings 3) incorrectly attributed to Hezekiah here (wrong_detail).

content: After keeping the Passover with great solemnity, what did the people of Israel do first when they returned to their cities?
options: Broke down the sacred pillars and demolished the high places of idols
Repaired the damaged city walls and gates
Offered thanksgiving sacrifices at their own homes
Compiled a census of the people by tribe
explanation: 2 Chronicles 31:1 records that the people of Israel went out to the cities of Judah and 'broke down the pillars, cut down the Asherah poles, and demolished the high places and the altars.' Repairing city walls was a later undertaking (wrong_detail). Offering sacrifices at private homes is not what the text describes (wrong_scope). Compiling a census by tribe was done in David's time, not this context (wrong_scope).

content: When King Hezekiah commanded the people of Jerusalem to give the portion due to the priests and Levites, what did the people bring in great abundance?
options: Gold, silver, and precious stones to rebuild the temple
The firstfruits of grain, wine, oil, honey, and all the produce of the field
Sheep and cattle for burnt offerings each morning
Fine linen and spices for worship
explanation: 2 Chronicles 31:5 records that the people brought in abundance 'the firstfruits of grain, wine, oil, honey, and of all the produce of the field,' along with a tithe of everything. Gold and silver to build the temple refers to a different occasion (wrong_detail). Sheep and cattle for burnt offerings were supplied by the king, not this particular contribution (near_passage). Fine linen and spices belonged to the tabernacle era, not this context (wrong_scope).

content: Why does the summary passage state that everything Hezekiah undertook prospered and succeeded?
options: Because the king sought God and wholeheartedly carried out the law and commandments
Because the king formed a military alliance with powerful Egypt for protection
Because the prophet Isaiah taught him privately in the temple every day
Because the king established a fair tax system that brought prosperity to the people
explanation: 2 Chronicles 31:21 records that 'in every work that he undertook... he sought his God with all his heart, and he prospered.' Allying with Egypt was something Isaiah rebuked, not a reason for success (common_misconception). Isaiah teaching daily in the temple is not mentioned in the text, even though Isaiah was a contemporary (true_but_off). Fair taxation sounds plausible but is not the reason the text provides (wrong_detail).

content: When Sennacherib advanced to attack, what defensive measure regarding water sources did Hezekiah discuss with his officials and warriors?
options: Dig new wells inside the city walls to store water
Stop up the springs and the brook that flowed through the land so the Assyrian army would find no water
Channel the waters of the Gihon spring into a reservoir between the two walls
Station guards at every well to prevent the city's residents from drawing water
explanation: 2 Chronicles 32:4 records that the people 'stopped all the springs and the brook that flowed through the land,' so that the king of Assyria would find no water when he came. Digging new wells inside is the reverse of what the text says (wrong_detail). Channeling Gihon's water into a pool belongs to verse 30 (the tunnel), not the measure described in verse 4 (near_passage). Stationing guards to prevent residents from drawing water is not in the text (wrong_scope).

content: Why did Hezekiah encourage the people not to fear the king of Assyria?
options: Because the walls of Jerusalem had been built up high and were very strong
Because with the king of Assyria is only an arm of flesh, but with the people is the LORD their God to help them
Because the army of Egypt was about to arrive to reinforce and rescue Judah
Because King Sennacherib was occupied with a rebellion that had broken out in his own land
explanation: 2 Chronicles 32:8 records Hezekiah saying, 'With him is an arm of flesh, but with us is the LORD our God, to help us and to fight our battles.' Strong walls were a preparation (verse 5) but not the stated reason for encouragement (near_passage). Egyptian reinforcements are not mentioned in the text (wrong_scope). Sennacherib facing a rebellion in his own land occurred later (verse 21), not this context (wrong_detail).

content: After being healed from a serious illness, Hezekiah made a mistake. What does the account reveal about the king's response and the consequences?
options: The king was proud so wrath came upon him, then he humbled himself so the calamity was postponed
The king was proud and did not humble himself, so the calamity came immediately in his lifetime
The king humbled himself immediately so God did not bring any wrath at all
The king displayed his treasures to the Babylonian envoys and was exiled in his own lifetime
explanation: 2 Chronicles 32:25-26 records that Hezekiah's heart was proud, 'so wrath came upon him and upon Judah and Jerusalem,' but then 'Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart,' so the wrath did not come during his lifetime. The option saying calamity came immediately overlooks his act of humbling himself (wrong_detail). The option saying God brought no wrath at all contradicts the text stating there 'was wrath' against him (common_misconception). The showing of treasures leading to exile is a later prophecy (v. 31 and Isaiah), not something that befell him in his own lifetime (true_but_off).

content: What engineering project of Hezekiah is recorded in connection with the water supply of Jerusalem?
options: He built a large reservoir outside the city walls to collect and store rainwater
He stopped the upper spring of the Gihon and directed it straight down to the west side of the city of David
He dug a long canal to bring water from the Jordan River into the city
He erected watchtowers along the streams flowing around the city of David
explanation: 2 Chronicles 32:30 records, 'It was Hezekiah who stopped the upper spring of the Gihon and directed it straight down to the west side of the city of David.' A reservoir outside the walls to collect rainwater is not mentioned in the text (wrong_detail). The Jordan River is far from Jerusalem and could not have been channeled into the city (common_misconception). Erecting watchtowers along streams is not the subject of this verse (wrong_scope).

content: How old was Manasseh when he became king of Judah, and how long did he reign in Jerusalem?
options: Twelve years old and reigned fifty-five years
Eight years old and reigned thirty-one years
Twenty-five years old and reigned twenty-nine years
Twenty-one years old and reigned two years
explanation: 2 Chronicles 33:1 records, 'Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem.' Eight years old and thirty-one years are the figures for Josiah (his son), not Manasseh (near_passage). Twenty-five years old is close to the figures for Amon or Jotham but incorrect (wrong_detail). Twenty-one years old and two years are the figures for Amon, Manasseh's son (near_passage).

content: What serious act of sacrilege by Manasseh is specifically mentioned as directly involving the temple itself?
options: The king burned the temple and plundered the golden vessels inside it
The king placed a carved idol in the house of God
The king shut the doors of the temple and extinguished the lamps in the sanctuary
The king removed the ark of the covenant from the Most Holy Place
explanation: 2 Chronicles 33:7 records that Manasseh 'set the carved image of the idol that he had made in the house of God.' The burning of the temple and plundering of its vessels occurred during the Babylonian invasion, which came later (wrong_scope). Shutting the temple doors and extinguishing the lamps was the sin of Ahaz, not Manasseh (near_passage). Removing the ark of the covenant from the Most Holy Place is not found in this text (wrong_detail).

content: Compared to his father Manasseh, what was the crucial difference in Amon that led to his end?
options: Amon sinned but did not humble himself and repent as his father had, and sinned even more
Amon worshiped idols but humbled himself at the end of his life just as his father had
Amon was more faithful than his father and destroyed the idols his father had erected
Amon was taken to Babylon and then brought back by God just as his father had been
explanation: 2 Chronicles 33:23 states the key contrast: 'he did not humble himself before the LORD, as Manasseh his father had humbled himself, but this Amon incurred guilt more and more,' and he was then killed by his servants (v. 24). The option saying Amon humbled himself at the end of his life like his father directly contradicts the text (common_misconception). The option saying Amon was more faithful and destroyed the idols contradicts the record that he sacrificed to them (wrong_detail). Being taken to Babylon and then brought back was Manasseh's experience, not Amon's (near_passage).

content: According to 2 Chronicles 34:1, how old was Josiah when he began to reign?
options: Eight years old
Twelve years old
Sixteen years old
Twenty-five years old
explanation: 2 Chronicles 34:1 states: 'Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign.' The option 'twelve years old' reflects the age at which Josiah began to seek God, as recorded in 34:3 — not the age he took the throne (wrong_detail). 'Sixteen years old' is not associated with any accession milestone in the text (wrong_detail). 'Twenty-five years old' is the accession age of a different king, not Josiah (wrong_scope).

content: According to 2 Chronicles 34:3–4, what did Josiah do with the altars of Baal and the carved idols during his religious reform?
options: Sealed them up for storage in a treasury
Tore them down and ground them to powder
Presented them to the priests as offerings
Transferred them to Assyria
explanation: 2 Chronicles 34:4 records that Josiah tore down the altars of Baal, broke the carved idols in pieces, and ground them to powder, scattering the dust over the graves of those who had sacrificed to them. 'Sealed them for storage' contradicts the total destruction described (wrong_detail). 'Presented them to the priests' confuses this act with lawful sacrificial offerings (common_misconception). 'Transferred them to Assyria' conflates the passage with the exile of the northern kingdom (wrong_scope).

content: According to 2 Chronicles 34:22, to which prophetess did Josiah send messengers to inquire of the LORD?
options: Deborah the prophetess
Miriam the sister of Moses
Huldah the prophetess
Anna the daughter of Phanuel
explanation: 2 Chronicles 34:22 records that the delegation went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum, to inquire of the LORD. 'Deborah' was a prophetess in the period of the Judges, a different era entirely (wrong_scope). 'Miriam' was a prophetess during the Exodus (wrong_scope). 'Anna' is a prophetess who appears in the New Testament (wrong_scope).

content: According to 2 Chronicles 36:1, after Josiah died, whom did the people of the land make king in Jerusalem in his place?
options: Jehoahaz son of Josiah
Jehoiakim son of Josiah
Zedekiah brother of Josiah
Jehoiachin grandson of Josiah
explanation: 2 Chronicles 36:1 states: 'The people of the land took Jehoahaz the son of Josiah and made him king in Jerusalem in his father's place.' Jehoiakim was installed by the king of Egypt shortly afterward (36:4), not by the people immediately following Josiah's death (near_passage). Zedekiah came to the throne last among Josiah's successors — and was a son, not a brother (wrong_detail). Jehoiachin reigned between Jehoiakim and Zedekiah (near_passage).

content: According to 2 Chronicles 34:26–28, why did the LORD promise that disaster would not come during Josiah's lifetime?
options: Because Josiah had offered many burnt offerings in the temple
Because Josiah's heart was tender and he humbled himself and wept before the LORD
Because Josiah had defeated the kings who worshiped idols
Because Josiah had rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem
explanation: 2 Chronicles 34:27 gives the LORD's own reason: 'because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before God... and you tore your clothes and wept before me.' Therefore the LORD heard him and withheld the disaster. 'Offering many burnt offerings' sounds consistent with Josiah's zeal but is not the reason the LORD explicitly cites (true_but_off). 'Defeating kings who worshiped idols' introduces military exploits not found in this passage (wrong_detail). 'Rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem' belongs to the work of Nehemiah, not Josiah (wrong_scope).

content: According to 2 Chronicles 35:20-22, what led to the death of Josiah at Megiddo?
options: He went to battle against King Neco despite being warned by a word from God
He was assassinated by a servant in the palace while he slept
He died of illness after keeping the Passover
He was surrounded and killed by the Babylonian army in battle
explanation: 2 Chronicles 35:21-22 records that Neco delivered a message from God, but Josiah did not listen, disguised himself, and went to fight at the Valley of Megiddo, where he was struck by archers. 'Assassinated by a servant while sleeping' confuses this with the manner of death of other kings such as Joash (wrong_detail). 'Died of illness' contradicts the account of him being struck by arrows in battle (wrong_detail). 'Killed by the Babylonian army' is wrong because his opponent was Neco king of Egypt, not Babylon (wrong_scope).

content: According to 2 Chronicles 35:25, after Josiah died, who composed a lament for him that became a custom observed in Israel?
options: The prophet Isaiah composed a song of victory
The prophet Jeremiah composed a lament
The Aaronic priests offered a prayer
King David composed a psalm of mourning
explanation: 2 Chronicles 35:25 records that 'Jeremiah also uttered a lament for Josiah' and that all the singing men and women have spoken of Josiah in their laments to this day. 'Isaiah composed a victory song' is wrong both in person and in character, since this is a funeral lament, not a triumphant hymn (wrong_detail). 'The Aaronic priests' are not identified as the authors of this lament (wrong_detail). 'David composed a psalm of mourning' is wrong in time period, as David lived hundreds of years before Josiah (wrong_scope).

content: According to 2 Chronicles 36:11-13, whom did King Zedekiah sin against when he broke the oath he had sworn by God?
options: Against the prophet Jeremiah
Against King Nebuchadnezzar
Against King Neco of Egypt
Against the priests in the temple
explanation: 2 Chronicles 36:13 records that Zedekiah 'rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God.' 'Against Jeremiah' sounds plausible because Zedekiah did oppose the prophet's words (36:12), but the oath was sworn to the king of Babylon (true_but_off). 'Against Neco of Egypt' confuses this with the adversary from the time of Josiah (wrong_scope). 'Against the priests' were not the party to whom the broken oath had been sworn (wrong_detail).

content: According to 2 Chronicles 34:29-33, after hearing the words of the Book of the Law, how did Josiah make a covenant, and what effect did it have on the people?
options: The king alone swore to keep the law, while the people remained free to worship as they pleased
The king made a covenant before the LORD and caused all those present to commit themselves to it
The king entrusted the making of the covenant to the high priest to act on his behalf
The king only commanded the elders while the common people had no part in it
explanation: 2 Chronicles 34:31-32 records that the king stood in his place and made a covenant before the LORD, then 'made all who were present in Jerusalem and in Benjamin join in it,' and throughout his lifetime the people did not turn away from following the LORD. 'The people remained free to worship as they pleased' directly contradicts the king binding all the people to the covenant (wrong_detail). 'Entrusted to the high priest to act on his behalf' is wrong because the king himself stood and made the covenant (wrong_detail). 'Only commanded the elders, the people had no part' sounds plausible given the gathering of the elders in 34:29, but contradicts the statement that 'all the people' committed themselves (near_passage).

content: According to 2 Chronicles 35:7-9, how did the king and the officials provide sacrificial animals to the people and the Levites during Josiah's Passover?
options: The people purchased their own sacrifices while the king only provided for the temple service
The king and the officials voluntarily gave lambs, young goats, and bulls to the people
Only the priests received sacrificial animals while the Levites had to provide for themselves
The sacrifices were purchased with silver taken from the Assyrian king's treasury
explanation: 2 Chronicles 35:7-9 records that Josiah gave the people lambs, young goats, and bulls, and then the officials and Levitical leaders also willingly contributed thousands of offerings to the people and the Levites. 'The people bought their own, the king only provided for the temple' contradicts the king's active provision of sacrificial animals (wrong_detail). 'Only the priests received offerings while the Levites provided for themselves' is wrong because the text explicitly states the offerings were given to the Levites as well (wrong_detail). 'Purchased with silver from the Assyrian king's treasury' introduces foreign financial details not present here, vaguely reminiscent of the silver for the temple repair in chapter 34 (near_passage).
